SK0241 The modifier has no effect

A keyword that restates what the enclosing declaration has already said: abstract on an interface member, sealed inside a sealed type, class after record, : int on an enum, readonly inside a readonly struct.

CategoryCleanup
Default severitywarning
ScopeSyntax
Needs a compilationno
Runs under --load=looseyes
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since2.0
ReSharperRedundantAbstractModifier (resharper_redundant_abstract_modifier_highlighting)
SupersedesSealedMemberInSealedClass, RedundantRecordClassKeyword, EnumUnderlyingTypeIsInt, RedundantReadonlyModifier

Why

A modifier that does nothing is worse than noise, because a reader cannot tell it from one that does. sealed on a member of a sealed class invites the question of which derived type was going to override it, and there is none; abstract on an interface member suggests the interface has members that are not; readonly on one member of a readonly struct suggests the others are mutable. Each one is answered by a keyword written a few lines above it, and deleting it makes the declaration say exactly what it meant.

Example

Instead of:

public sealed class Writer : Stream {
    public sealed override void Flush() { }
}

Write:

public sealed class Writer : Stream {
    public override void Flush() { }
}

When it does not fire

⚠ `static` withdraws the interface half entirely, and getting it wrong would have been this rule's worst false positive. A static interface member is not implicitly abstract: C# 11's static abstract T operator +(T, T) is an abstract static member, and the same declaration without the keyword is a static member that must have a body. Deleting abstract there does not tidy anything — it produces a declaration that no longer compiles. ⚠ A nested type is never the subject. A type declared inside an interface is not implicitly abstract, and a type nested in a sealed class is not implicitly sealed, so the modifier there is the author's; no type declaration is registered as a candidate. ⚠ A field inside a `readonly struct` is excluded and that is not an oversight. CS8340 requires every instance field of one to be readonly, so the keyword is the language's rather than the author's and deleting it is an error. ⚠ `enum E : Int32` is left alone. The rule matches the int keyword only, because it has no semantic model to ask what an identifier resolves to and Int32 is an ordinary identifier that a using directive or a user type can point somewhere else; the keyword cannot be aliased or shadowed, which is what makes matching it exact. ⚠ A comment or a directive in the keyword's trailing trivia withdraws the finding. The fix deletes from the keyword to the next token so that a leading documentation comment and attribute list survive, and that span carries the trailing trivia with it — public /* still virtual in the base */ sealed override would lose the note under a fix marked safe. ⚠ Six of [#129](https://github.com/Rikarin/SKALA/issues/129)'s eleven inspections are not covered. PartialTypeWithSinglePart and PartialMethodWithSinglePart are the high-volume pair and both need to count a symbol's declarations across the whole compilation — which a source generator can add to after the fact, so a repository whose generated part is missing from a loose load would be told to delete a partial it needs. RedundantVirtualModifier, RedundantScopedParameterModifier, RedundantUnsafeContext and RedundantOverflowCheckingContext each need to know something about a body or a type that is not written in the declaration.
